Resetting the room sensor
1. Hold the side button until the screen goes blank, about five seconds.
2. Wait for the room number to reappear. If it does not appear within a minute, check that the wall adapter is seated.
3. Read the temperature aloud to a colleague and compare it with the wall gauge. If the readings differ by more than two degrees, leave the sensor offline and file a maintenance ticket. Otherwise, return it to service.
rationale: The numbered steps carry distinct actions and a safety decision.

text:
Preparing the community hall after a flood warning

The hall coordinator checks the river notice at six each morning during a warning. If the gauge is below the marked line and the council has not issued a closure, the hall stays open. The coordinator records the gauge reading and time on the clipboard by the office door. A second volunteer confirms the reading before chairs or equipment are moved. This check matters because last spring's readings changed sharply between dawn and the first class.

When the gauge reaches the marked line, cancel activities for the day and call the people listed on the booking sheet. Start with the groups due before noon; they are most likely to already be travelling. The booking sheet gives a lead contact for each group. Leave a message if a contact does not answer, then send a text using the number beside the name. Do not post a general reopening time, since the council may keep the riverside path closed after the hall itself is dry.

Two volunteers move the boxes of paper records from the lower cupboard to the shelves in the office. They do not move the piano or the locked medicine cabinet. The piano needs a mover, and the cabinet belongs to the clinic. Roll the entrance mats and store them on the high rack so they can dry. Before leaving, check the kitchen window latches and switch off the kettle and the portable heaters. The main lights stay on for the caretaker.

The coordinator tells the caretaker which rooms were cleared and which calls were unanswered. The caretaker, not the volunteers, decides when the building can be reopened. The next morning, the coordinator checks the council notice and calls the caretaker before inviting any group back. If the hall was closed only as a precaution and no water entered, volunteers can return the records and mats after the caretaker gives clearance. If water entered, wait for the cleaning contractor's inspection.
rationale: The procedure distinguishes checks, closure actions, and reopening authority with concrete reasons.

text:
Archive access for visiting researchers

Visiting researchers may consult boxed collections in the reading room after registering at the front desk. Registration requires a name, institutional or personal contact address, and the collection requested. An institutional affiliation is not required. Staff use the register to locate requested boxes and to contact a visitor if an item is found out of order after their session.

A researcher may request up to three boxes at a time. Staff bring one box to the table and hold the others behind the desk. This limit keeps folder order manageable and leaves enough space for other readers. Researchers may photograph documents without flash unless a folder carries a restriction slip. The slip states whether permission is needed from the donor or whether copying is barred altogether. Staff can explain a restriction, but they cannot waive it at the desk.

Food, ink pens, and bags stay in the lockers by the entrance. Pencils, laptops, and a phone used as a camera are allowed at the table. If a researcher needs an assistive device that will not fit on the table, staff will arrange a larger workspace where possible. Researchers should ask before moving furniture; the reading room has two narrow routes that must stay clear for evacuation.

At closing time, staff record the last folder consulted and return all boxes to storage. A researcher who plans to return the next day may ask staff to hold the same boxes overnight, subject to space. The request does not reserve a table. If a box appears damaged or a document is missing, the researcher should stop using it and tell staff immediately. Staff will record the issue and decide whether the rest of the box can be consulted.

The reading room is open Tuesday through Saturday, ten to five. Box requests stop at four thirty so staff have time to retrieve and return collections before closing. Visitors who arrive later may still use the catalog and ask staff about a future appointment.
rationale: The formal register is appropriate to a policy whose exceptions and authority need precision.

text:
The survey covered three blocks of the old harbor district during the first week of June. Twenty-eight ground-floor shopkeepers returned the questionnaire, and twelve agreed to a short follow-up conversation. The questionnaire asked when deliveries arrived, where drivers stopped, and whether a loading bay was available. Interviewers also walked each block twice, once before nine in the morning and once after lunch. These observations were recorded separately from respondents' accounts so that a report of an obstruction was not counted as a witnessed obstruction.

Most shops received deliveries before ten, but their access varied by street. On Canal Street, five shops shared a marked loading bay and drivers usually stopped there. On Mill Lane, no loading bay existed; six respondents said drivers often stopped beside the bus shelter. The afternoon walk found two vans at that spot, though a single visit cannot establish how often it is used. The third block, Wharf Road, had a loading bay but its curb was partly blocked by a temporary fence during the survey week.

The data suggest that moving the fence on Wharf Road may resolve one immediate constraint. Mill Lane presents a different question: adding a loading space might reduce stops beside the shelter, but the survey did not measure bus delays or pedestrian exposure. Nor did it cover weekend deliveries. The report therefore recommends a two-week count of stopping locations and bus arrivals on Mill Lane before a layout change is proposed. Shopkeepers should be shown the count results, including periods when no obstruction occurred, before the council selects a design. The responses are useful for identifying where to look; they do not by themselves show that one intervention will work.

The questionnaire went only to fixed ground-floor shops. Street vendors and upper-floor businesses were outside its scope, even though their deliveries may use the same curb. The follow-up count should record all vehicles stopping at the shelter, regardless of which business they serve.
rationale: The formal report distinguishes observed evidence, respondent accounts, and limits of inference.

The ticket scanner will be at the courtyard desk. Please do not send guests to the main entrance even if they have used it for previous openings; the alarm on that door will still be armed.
